title: Trump asks Supreme Court to overturn $83.3 million award in E. Jean Carroll defamation case
summary: Lawyers for President Donald Trump argued that he had immunity for statements made while president.
story: President Donald Trump is again asking the Supreme Court to intervene in his yearslong legal battle with writer E. Jean Carroll, this time arguing that he should not have to pay an $83.3 million jury award on the grounds of presidential immunity.

Lawyers for Trump urged the high court to review the case and consider overturning the jury’s ruling in 2024 that found he defamed Carroll after he repeatedly denied that he sexually abused her in a dressing room in 1996.

“This is the first case in our Nation’s history in which a court has imposed damages liability on a President for his conduct in office,” Trump’s lawyers wrote in the filing, calling the $83.3 million award “exorbitant.”
“If left standing, the decision below will cause significant damage, not only to this President and future Presidents, but also to ‘the Nation that the Presidency was designed to serve,’” they wrote.

Carroll sued Trump in 2019 over allegations that he defamed her during his first term in office, including when he said she made up the allegations of sexual abuse to sell more copies of her upcoming book.

Trump’s lawyers argued Tuesday that under the Westfall Act, a federal statute that protects government employees from certain lawsuits while they are engaged in their official duties, Trump should be able to swap out his name as the defendant in the case and replace it with the U.S. government.
If it is applied, the act would essentially nullify Carroll’s case, since the U.S. government cannot be sued for defamation.

“Here, the president of the United States has been ordered to pay nearly $100 million in damages ... for issuing a press release and answering reporters’ questions, from the White House, defending against attacks on his fitness for office,” the filing said.

Trump’s lawyers argued that the “threat of even a single damages judgment based on official acts will render all Presidents ‘unable to boldly and fearlessly carry out [their] duties for fear that [they] may be next.’”
Trump asked a federal appeals court to consider his argument for presidential immunity in the case in April when his lawyers requested a rehearing before a full bench of judges.
The appeals court denied the request, as did a three-judge panel that rejected an appeal from Trump in September that was based on presidential immunity.
Trump’s lawyers pushed back against the appeals court’s ruling in the filing Tuesday, citing the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision on presidential immunity.

The filing said the appeals court “refused to apply Presidential immunity even after this Court recognized that ‘most of a President’s public communications are likely to fall comfortably within’ that protection.”
Carroll’s legal team declined to comment on the petition Tuesday evening.
The Supreme Court denied Trump’s request last month to review a separate successful defamation lawsuit filed by Carroll.

That case, which was filed in 2022 after her initial lawsuit was delayed by legal questions, focused on the sexual abuse itself and on claims that Trump defamed her after he left office. A jury awarded Carroll $5 million in the second case in 2023.
Carroll collected the award from that judgment this month after Trump tried repeatedly to block the payment in court. Trump has denied all wrongdoing in both cases.

title: South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden fends off challenger in GOP primary runoff
summary: NBC News projects that Rhoden, who replaced Kristi Noem last year, defeated businessman Toby Doeden to win the Republican nomination for governor.
story: South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden has won his Republican primary, NBC News projects, after he was forced into a runoff in his bid for a full term in office.
He defeated businessman and political newcomer Toby Doeden in a one-on-one matchup Tuesday after no candidate won 35% of the vote in the initial June primary.

Rhoden will face off in the November general election against Democrat Dan Ahlers, a former state senator, in the solidly red state. South Dakota has not had a Democratic governor since the 1970s, and its two U.S. senators and lone House member are all Republicans.

Rhoden previously was lieutenant governor and was elevated to the top job after President Donald Trump selected then-Gov. Kristi Noem to be homeland security secretary. (She was fired this year.) Now, Rhoden aims to secure his first full term as governor.

Doeden won about 31% of the vote in the June primary, while Rhoden took about 25%. Rep. Dusty Johnson and state House Speaker Jon Hansen also sought the nomination, but neither received enough support to advance to the runoff.

Rhoden and Doeden positioned themselves as strong allies of Trump, who did not make an endorsement in the primary. Rhoden framed himself as a candidate with “the proven track record of uniting Republicans from all factions,” while Doeden argued that the state “needs bold conservative leadership, not career politicians.”

Rhoden campaigned on cutting property taxes and crime and touted the state’s unemployment rate, the lowest in the country. Doeden ran on reducing property taxes, as well as deporting migrants, supporting rural communities and opposing diversity, equity and inclusion efforts in the state.

Doeden, who poured his own money into his campaign, outspent Rhoden on the airwaves in the runoff. Rhoden also faced attack ads calling him a “career politician” from a super PAC tied to the conservative Club for Growth, which did not publicly endorse in the race.

title: Two Democrats advance to a runoff in the Georgia special election to succeed late Rep. David Scott
summary: Scott’s daughter Marcye Scott and fellow Democrat Everton Blair finished atop a five-candidate field, but no one got majority support, triggering the runoff, NBC News projects.
story: Marcye Scott, the daughter of the late Rep. David Scott, and fellow Democrat Everton Blair advanced to a runoff Tuesday in the Georgia special election to fill the final months of the longtime congressman’s term in the House, NBC News projects.
The two candidates finished atop a five-candidate, all-party special primary election for Georgia’s 13th District. But since no one got majority support, the race will go one more round.
With about 80% of the expected vote tallied, Marcye Scott had 47% support and Blair, a former school board chair in Gwinnett County, had 37%.
David Scott died April 22, triggering the special election to decide who holds the seat for the rest of 2026.
He represented the solid-blue district, consisting of counties covering metro Atlanta and southern suburbs, for two decades and won his final term with about 72% support in the 2024 election.

Voters in the district already participated in a separate contest for the next full congressional term in the 13th District starting in January. Jasmine Clark, a state legislator, won that Democratic primary this year, about four weeks after David Scott died.
Marcye Scott and Blair outran a field that included one other Democrat, Carlos Moore, and two Republicans, Caesar Gonzales and Fayth Park.

title: Has cyclospora outbreak peaked? There are promising signs in Michigan after lettuce recall.
summary: There are promising signs that illnesses linked to contaminated lettuce may be slowing in Michigan, the hot spot of the multistate outbreak of cyclosporiasis in the U.S.
story: There are promising signs that illnesses linked to contaminated lettuce may be slowing in Michigan, the hot spot of the multistate outbreak of cyclosporiasis in the U.S. That doesn’t mean all the affected produce is gone from stores or restaurants, or that more people aren’t still getting sick, experts say.

On Tuesday, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported more than 18,000 confirmed or suspected nationwide cases of cyclosporiasis, the illness caused by a parasite found in human feces. In nine states, most of the illnesses have been traced to shredded iceberg lettuce sourced from Taylor Farms de Mexico. Other states, such as New York and North Carolina, have also seen higher-than-normal clusters, from unknown sources.
The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services said Tuesday that more than 9,500 people have gotten sick from the parasite in the state, with about 160 hospitalizations, in the last two months.
The Food and Drug Administration didn’t immediately respond to questions about its progress in tracing the source or sources of the illness.
It has been over a week since Taylor Farms voluntarily recalled iceberg lettuce from some Taco Bell restaurants, groceries and food service suppliers.

While the outbreak isn’t over in Michigan, cases may have peaked there. Dr. Natasha Bagdasarian, the state’s chief medical executive, said a significant number of recently reported cases, roughly 475 since Friday, were a result of a reporting delay at one particular healthcare system and don’t necessarily reflect new illnesses.
Bagdasarian said another positive indicator they are seeing is that the percentage of visits to emergency departments with diarrhea as a main complaint is slowing.
However, people with milder symptoms may not be getting tested.

“I do have a big caveat,” said Bagdasarian. “We have heard recently from some of our health systems that because of backlogs in their labs, and because of limitations with testing supplies, they have been limiting tests to those who are severely ill, or those who are immunocompromised.”
Because of this limitation, investigators in Michigan are unsure about the projected spread of cyclospora, especially if other, unidentified culprits are still in the food supply.
“I don’t know if a single product recall is related to the slowdown that we’ve seen,” said Bagdasarian.

While the purportedly contaminated lettuce has been recalled, Bagdasarian also credited public health interventions, such as guidance to peel, cook and remove the outer layers of produce, for the slowdown.
Bagdasarian said it’s up to the federal health agencies to trace, test and find the contaminated produce, based on interviews with patients and other data gathering.

“There are a fair number of folks out there who have not reported eating lettuce or who have not reported eating at any particular fast-food restaurant,” she said. “So I don’t know, based on my data, that I can think this is exclusively lettuce or whether there are other things going on, especially knowing that there are multiple other outbreaks happening across the United States.”
Health officials don’t have access to real-time genetic sequencing, which makes it harder to match a contaminated product to a specific case.

Jennifer McEntire, the founder of Food Safety Strategy, a consulting firm, said it’s also difficult to pinpoint a specific source because many products “move or change hands many times, go through numerous distribution centers [and] sometimes brokers.”

Health officials have suspected other food sources in this season’s outbreaks, namely cilantro and parsley, but have not confirmed either one. In New York, state officials investigated an earlier, smaller cluster of cyclosporiasis cases in April and traced the outbreak to cilantro served at a Brooklyn restaurant, though they never definitively confirmed it was the source.

Last week, officials in North Carolina — which has reported 561 cyclospora cases — said their preliminary investigation suggests cilantro and parsley could be behind those cases. Neither state’s outbreaks have been linked to Taylor Farms lettuce.

Dr. Stephen Ostroff, a former acting FDA commissioner, said it’s possible other illnesses could stem from contaminated lettuce that was grown in the same region as Taylor Farms de Mexico and was also served in the U.S.
Frank Yiannas, former deputy commissioner for food policy and response at the FDA, said it’s clear there is more than one product causing illnesses.

“If, in fact, all the lettuce is pulled from the market, consumers should not be surprised that they continue to see states report illnesses, and they identify food vehicles other than lettuce,” he said.

In Michigan, there have been two distinct waves of cyclospora, which tends to be a summer problem in the U.S. This year, the first wave peaked June 21 through June 28, and again July 5 through July 12, Bagdasarian said.

Barbara Kowalcyk, director of the Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security at George Washington University, believes that’s because the contaminated product was supplied in two separate batches.
“If you have ongoing contamination of irrigation water or processing water, then you will see the outbreak going on,” she said.
“So the question that raises in my mind is: Is there a larger contamination event in that part of the country?” Kowalcyk said, referring to the Taylor Farms site in central Mexico.
Contaminated water has the potential to spread to different crops and multiple batches of products.
“There’s still a lot that we don’t know,” said Kowalcyk. “This goes back to the need for better laboratory methods in terms of detecting cyclospora in the environment.”
Kowalcyk said that the continued search for the source of the cyclospora outbreak highlights vulnerabilities in the U.S.’ public health system, a result of a lack of funding.
“We still need increased capacity. We aren’t investing enough in science. We’re not investing enough in research,” Kowalcyk said.

title: Senate confirms Jay Clayton as new director of intelligence
summary: The Senate approved federal prosecutor Jay Clayton as the next director of national intelligence.
story: WASHINGTON — The Senate approved President Donald Trump’s choice to oversee the country’s spy agencies, with the Republican majority voting Tuesday to install top federal prosecutor Jay Clayton as the next director of national intelligence.

Clayton, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York in Manhattan, will inherit a much smaller agency after his predecessors cut the office’s workforce in a series of firings in recent weeks and months. And his confirmation follows accusations from Democratic lawmakers and former national security officials that the Trump White House has tried to use the intelligence agencies to wage partisan political warfare.
The vote was 51-47 along party lines.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google

After Clayton was confirmed, Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., the Intelligence Committee’s vice chairman, explained why he voted against the nomination in a statement and expressed hope that Clayton would not cave to possible political pressure from the White House.

“Having known and worked with Jay for years, I was encouraged when he was first nominated for the position of DNI,” Warner said. “Unfortunately, I came away from his confirmation process with serious reservations about whether he would be willing to stand up to political pressure when it matters most.”
The Republican leader of the Intelligence Committee, Tom Cotton of Arkansas, welcomed the vote in favor of Clayton.

“Jay Clayton is a highly qualified nominee with a deep experience combatting a wide range of national security threats,” Cotton said in a statement. “As U.S. attorney, Mr. Clayton has worked hand in glove with our intelligence agencies and counterterrorism personnel to lock up criminals who threaten our national security.”

Hours earlier, the acting intelligence chief, Bill Pulte, announced on social media what he called a fifth round of job cuts at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence since he took office in June. But he did not say how many positions were cut or how many employees were fired or merely reassigned to other intelligence agencies.
Pulte described the move as “an approximately 30% Staff Reduction from Weeks Ago.”

The National Intelligence Director’s Office had roughly 2,000 employees at the start of Trump’s second term last year, and his first director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, had proposed cuts in the workforce of about 40%. The 30% reduction Pulte cited could put the current workforce at about 1,000, former officials said.
The National Intelligence Director’s Office and the White House declined to comment.
A spokesperson for Warner said Pulte has failed to share with lawmakers information about workforce reductions or a rationale for the cuts.

“The Acting DNI has been quick to announce firings and make public claims about them, but has so far declined to provide the Senate Intelligence Committee with the information necessary to assess the accuracy of those statements or the basis for those decisions,” said Rachel Cohen, Warner’s communications director.

Congress created the national intelligence director’s position in the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks with the aim of ensuring that information was shared across the country’s spy agencies.
But Trump and some Republican lawmakers have called for scaling back the office, which they say has become a bloated bureaucracy.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
Clayton enjoys stronger support among Republican lawmakers than Pulte, a Trump loyalist who came to the job without relevant national security experience.

At his confirmation hearing this month, Clayton refused to say who won the 2020 election, sidestepping questions that could put him at odds with Trump. Trump has repeatedly claimed without evidence that the 2020 election, which Joe Biden won, was rigged.

Democrats on the Intelligence Committee said Clayton’s answers raised doubts about whether he would provide accurate information to Trump if it was out of line with his views or whether he would protect spy agencies from possible political manipulation.
Trump picked Pulte to succeed Gabbard after she said she was resigning because of her husband’s cancer diagnosis.
Pulte won Trump’s approval as head of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, where he launched investigations into Trump’s perceived political enemies.

title: Top scientists at OpenAI and Anthropic ask U.S. for tools to pace AI development
summary: More than 1,000 employees at America’s leading AI companies signed a statement asking the U.S. to help support efforts to “pace” cutting-edge AI development.
story: More than 1,000 employees at America’s leading AI companies, including senior staff members and some co-founders at OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind, signed a statement asking the U.S. government to help support international efforts to “deliberately pace” cutting-edge automated AI development.

Highlighting recent comments from the world’s most advanced AI companies that AI systems may soon be able to automate their own research and development, the statement calls on the U.S. government to help create technical and policy tools that could control automated AI progress in coordination with other companies and countries.

“To realize AI’s potential, industry, government, and society at large may need the option to buy time to address emerging risks, develop security measures, and strengthen oversight,” the statement says.
“We request that the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development,” it concludes.

The statement does not explicitly call for the government or AI companies to slow or pause AI development, as some AI advocates have proposed; instead, it asks political leaders to ensure that option is simply available as AI development continues.
Bloomberg first reported the letter was circulating among AI company employees.

OpenAI said last week that its latest, unreleased model escaped its testing environment and went rogue, attacking an unrelated AI service provider in an attempt to achieve a higher score on an internal test. Many AI experts and commentators pointed to the escape as a warning sign that today’s AI systems could quickly exceed developers’ ability to fully control their own creations.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who did not sign the letter, said this week on a taping of the “Relentless” podcast that humans are now “in the singularity,” often referred to as the point at which AI becomes able to autonomously improve itself. He did not provide further detail or evidence that such an inflection point had been reached.

Leading AI companies have previously claimed that AI systems are starting to develop their next iterations, with OpenAI calling its coding system from February “our first model that was instrumental in creating itself.” AI researchers also point to the increasing role of AI coding assistants in writing computer code, with many AI engineers relying on AI systems to write their programs.

Tuesday’s statement was signed by the chief scientists or science officers from Anthropic (Jared Kaplan), OpenAI (Jakub Pachocki) and Meta (Shengjia Zhao), along with senior leaders from Google and Thinking Machines, a key Silicon Valley AI startup founded by OpenAI veterans.

Many of the developers and scientists who signed the statement say they have been routinely startled by the speed of AI development. “I have worked in AI for a decade,” said Stephanie Chan, a staff research scientist at Google. “Every few months in the last years, I have found myself surprised again and again at how rapidly the technology advances, no matter how often I update my predictions.”

Key research tasks required to develop stronger AI systems can now be performed by AI agents, or autonomous AI systems, themselves, though human researchers are still heavily involved in checking the agents’ work and setting overall research directions.

Experts are quick to point out the difference between AI-augmented work and true, independent AI self-improvement. Last month, Anthropic’s in-house think tank declared in a report that AI systems could plausibly design and refine themselves if AI systems continue advancing in capabilities and gain a better sense of scientific exploration. At the time, Anthropic said “it would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development” to give society time to prepare for automated AI R&D.

Other groups have explicitly focused on continuously self-improving models as the next goal for AI development, though many AI experts fear that sort of self-improvement could quickly cause AI systems to spiral out of human control. While such events could seem like science fiction worries, experts say AI’s current trajectory could make that sort of loss-of-control scenario come to life.

“Many researchers also consider recursive self-improvement (RSI) plausible within the next few years, accelerating progress in a way that could outpace our ability to understand and govern these systems,” Dawn Song, Meta’s vice president of AI research and a professor of computer science at the University of California, Berkeley, wrote in a comment published alongside Tuesday’s statement. “Preparing before a crisis is the prudent path.”
Tuesday’s letter calls for increased American involvement in international collaboration on “technical and governance tools” to pace AI’s development.

While the Trump administration has inveighed against international AI governance, arguing that such attempts could instead unfairly constrain American innovation, that isolationist approach may have changed over the past few months.

As AI has emerged as a key national security issue, with Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT 5.6 Sol AI models proving able to find and exploit novel cybersecurity vulnerabilities, the U.S. has pursued international agreements to shore up its chip supply chains and worked with allies to ensure that key AI equipment does not fall into adversaries’ hands.
Leo Gao, who has focused on safety efforts at OpenAI since 2021, wrote in a comment Tuesday that international coordination on technical and policy tools could help defuse dangerous AI tensions.

“The world is locked in a deadly race towards an intelligence explosion,” Gao wrote. “Going slower would give us much-needed time to make it go well, but no individual actor is willing to stop unilaterally. To survive, we must coordinate to slow down the race.”

title: Ghost gun recovered in deadly Seattle festival shooting
summary: Seattle officials said that the teen suspect may have been using a ghost gun and that they want to hear from one person who was treated for gunshot wounds.
story: A loaded “ghost gun” was recovered at the scene of a deadly Seattle shooting over the weekend, police said Tuesday as they continue to search for a possible third suspect.

The weapon was found on a 15-year-old who is suspected of being one of the shooters Sunday at the Bite of Seattle food festival, where three people were killed and four were injured. The teen was taken into custody and remains in juvenile detention, according to police.

Ghost guns are firearms that can be assembled at home from parts purchased online. The parts are often obtained without background checks and do not have serial numbers, which would make the guns traceable.

Police found a polymer 89 mm firearm with an extended magazine. It had a 33-round capacity, and 19 rounds remained in the magazine when investigators retrieved it, Police Chief Shon Barnes said at a news conference Tuesday afternoon.
A second gun, which police do not believe was used in the shooting, was found with a full seven rounds in its standard magazine.
Police retrieved a third gun, a Glock Model 45 9 mm pistol with a fully automatic switch. Twenty-one of 40 rounds remained in the magazine, Barnes said.
In total, 14 shell casings from two weapons were found at the scene. The guns had not been reported stolen, police said.
“We have dozens of pieces of digital evidence to review and are continuing to review that information as well as searching the area for more,” Barnes told reporters.
Since Sunday night, the Seattle Police Department has received more than 80 calls to its tip line, Barnes said.

Investigators have said there may have been a third person in the gunbattle, which they say also included the 15-year-old and his 19-year-old “associate,” Junior Cee Niko Semo, who died of multiple gunshot wounds.

The shooting began shortly after 6 p.m. Sunday at the popular food festival, near the famous Space Needle. Two bystanders — Ashley Whitehead, 56, and Carlos Israel Sanchez Villalba, 44 — were killed by gunfire.
Four other people sustained non-life-threatening injuries.

Police said there could be an additional survivor who self-reported to a local hospital with a gunshot wound and then left after having been treated. Because of “legal barriers,” Barnes said, police do not know the person’s identity.

“If you are that person, please reach out to us,” he said. “We would like to make sure, No. 1, that you’re OK, and No. 2, if you would like to speak to an investigator, please reach out to us so we can determine if you may have seen what happened.”

How to choose a meat delivery service

The first factor you’ll want to consider is the type of meat offered. While various services specialize in specific types — for example, Omaha Steaks is known for its high-quality cuts of steak and beef — many offer a range of beef, poultry, pork and even seafood. That being said, your personal preference is most important in this case, so you’ll want to look for a service that specializes in your favorite types, or at least has a wide enough selection that you’ll be able to find the cuts you’re looking for.

According to Pierrel, two non-negotiables for raising meat are avoiding antibiotics and added hormones. Adding hormones is banned in chicken but still legal in beef, so Pierrel suggests checking for third-party verification, like the USDA Process Verified shield, which shows that a brand’s processes have been independently audited by the USDA.

She also says it’s important to understand these various certifications. “Words like ‘premium’, ‘natural,’ and ‘butcher’s cut’ have no legal definition; they just sound official,” she says. However, there are a few terms she suggests keeping an eye out for when looking at how your meat was raised.

Grass-fed and pasture-raised labels are great to look for if your budget allows it (since they tend to be a bit pricier). While grass-fed tells you what an animal ate, pasture-raised ensures the animal lived unconfined, outside of the grazing area, says Pierrel. “That combination produces meat that’s more nutrient-dense per bite, with a higher omega-3 profile, so it satisfies you with less,” she says. For an insider tip, she recommends looking for grass-finished meat as well, since it guarantees grass for life, unlike the grass-fed labeling.USDA Organic is the federally inspected certification that guarantees the meat has been fed organically, with no pesticides, antibiotics or added hormones, and real access to pastures, says Pierrel. However, since the certification process can be expensive, a lot of high-quality, smaller farms may skip the process. There are pros and cons to both fresh and frozen meat, according to the experts. The choice will ultimately depend on your personal preferences and uses for the meat.

Fresh meat is great for meals you’ll be preparing right away or in the days soon after your delivery. Usually, being able to cook the meat right away will result in a better texture and flavor, says Kais. However, since it has a shorter shelf life, it needs to be enjoyed quickly. Fresh meat also ages through transit, whereas frozen meat is flash frozen right after processing, which preserves it at its peak, says Pierrel.Frozen meat is an excellent alternative to fresh, especially from a nutritional and safety standpoint. The flash-freezing not only helps preserve quality and nutrients, but reduces the risk of spoilage during transit as well, says Kais. Pierrel says it’s also “the smarter way to stock up”, since you can save it for later in your freezer, while Kais adds that it often also provides more selection, since specialty cuts may not be available fresh. The only con is that frozen meats can sometimes experience changes in texture after thawing; however, Kais says that it shouldn’t be a major issue if handled properly (and in my experience, I had no issues with texture).

The regulatory oversight for shipping frozen meats is handled by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the Food and Safety Inspection Service (FSIS). Below, I’ve outlined a few requirements for safe meat delivery packaging for fresh and frozen meat.

Fresh meat needs to arrive at your door below 40 degrees Fahrenheit, since bacteria develop fastest in what the USDA calls the Danger Zone, which is between 40 degrees and 140 degrees Fahrenheit, says Pierrel. Since you can’t see, smell or taste that bacterial growth, she warns that you shouldn’t gamble with your meat if you’re unsure. Beef in the US is graded by the USDA, and primarily focuses on marbling, which is the intramuscular fat that’s woven inside of the muscle, according to experts. “Marbling is important because it melts during cooking, helping keep the meat more tender and flavorful,” says Kais. However, Pierrel says that many shoppers aren’t aware of exactly how the grading is assessed. “The grade is assessed on the ribeye, between the 12th and 13th ribs, the fattiest section of the animal, and that single measurement grades the entire carcass, so every cut from that animal is sold under it,” she says. Since the grade measures taste, rather than nutrition or lifestyle conditions, leaner grass-fed and pasture-raised options may be graded lower simply for the lower fat content. Given that, she suggests looking at those kinds of meat, along with USDA Organic meat, if you’re more concerned with nutrition and animal welfare. “The best steak is the one that matches your goal,” she says.
The USDA grades meat into Prime, Choice and Select categories, with Prime being the highest, says Kais.

How I picked the best hair sunscreens

Experts agree that you should be protecting both your scalp and hair. For your scalp, choose a broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher in sprays, lightweight lotions, sticks and brush-on mineral powders, depending on your hairstyle and hair density. For the hair shaft, look for lightweight leave-in UV protectants that help prevent damage, moisture loss and color fading without making your hair greasy, says Dr. Kseniya Kobets, director of cosmetic dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care Cosmetic Dermatology Center.
When shopping for a hair SPF, the dermatologists I spoke to recommend considering the following factors:

Broad-spectrum protection: Look for UV-protectant sprays or mists that clearly state “broad-spectrum protection” on the label. “These products create a protective barrier on the hair shaft and help reflect UV radiation away from the strands,” says board-certified cosmetic dermatologist Dr. Michele Green.Consistency: Choose a lightweight, non-greasy formula that won’t weigh your hair down or leave any residue. “Heavier sunscreen products designed for the skin can make hair appear oily or feel sticky. UV-filtering sprays and mists are best because they distribute evenly without disrupting your hairstyle,” says Green. Additionally, powder sunscreens with SPF can protect the scalp along the part line without adding any oil.Nourishing ingredients: Consider leave-in treatments that combine UV filters with nourishing ingredients like antioxidants or plant oils. “You’ll get both protection and added hydration in one convenient step,” says Green.

Broad-spectrum protection: Look for UV-protectant sprays or mists that clearly state “broad-spectrum protection” on the label. “These products create a protective barrier on the hair shaft and help reflect UV radiation away from the strands,” says board-certified cosmetic dermatologist Dr. Michele Green.

Consistency: Choose a lightweight, non-greasy formula that won’t weigh your hair down or leave any residue. “Heavier sunscreen products designed for the skin can make hair appear oily or feel sticky. UV-filtering sprays and mists are best because they distribute evenly without disrupting your hairstyle,” says Green. Additionally, powder sunscreens with SPF can protect the scalp along the part line without adding any oil.

Nourishing ingredients: Consider leave-in treatments that combine UV filters with nourishing ingredients like antioxidants or plant oils. “You’ll get both protection and added hydration in one convenient step,” says Green.
Do you need sunscreen for your hair?

Unlike your scalp, which needs SPF because you’re protecting skin from sunburn, premature aging and skin cancer, the hair shaft benefits from UV protection primarily for cosmetic reasons. Hair is made of keratin, which UV rays can damage over time, similar to how sun exposure breaks down collagen in the skin and leaves it weaker, says Green. The sun can strip your hair of its natural oils, fade its color and make it more susceptible to breakage and split ends. “This is particularly important for individuals with color-treated, chemically processed, or already damaged hair, as these types tend to be more porous and therefore more vulnerable to UV-related harm,” says Green.

Hair UV protectants, sometimes called Hair Protection Factor, help preserve color, strength, shine and smoothness. These are usually hair products, like leave-in conditioners, with built-in UV filters. “They’re especially helpful if you spend a lot of time outdoors or swim frequently,” says Kobets.

However, experts agree that physical protection, like wearing a wide-brimmed hat or wrapping your head in a scarf, can be more beneficial than a product with UV protection because they shield both your hair and scalp from direct sun exposure.
Frequently asked questions

Just like the skin on the rest of your body, your scalp is at risk of damage from the sun. “It can burn, age prematurely, develop precancerous lesions and increase your risk of skin cancer just like the rest of your body,” says Kobets. “This is especially important if you have thinning hair, part your hair down the middle, have a visible part or are bald.”

As for your hair shaft, the sun breaks down keratin, dries it out (UVB damage) and breaks down the color (UVA damage), says double board-certified facial plastic and reconstructive surgeon Dr. Jamie DeRosa. Sun damage can cause your hair to look dry, brittle and straw-like.

While you can spray or apply your favorite sunscreen onto your scalp, be prepared for your hair to look greasy and matted, says Evans. Traditional sunscreens are designed to sit on your skin and usually have heavier oils, waxes or thick emollients, which can make your hair look greasy, weighed down or coated with residue, says Green. They also don’t wash out easily, which can lead to buildup on your scalp, clogged hair follicles or irritation.
Instead, apply traditional sunscreen along your exposed hairline or on parts of the ears and neck that aren’t covered by hair, which are areas that still require standard SPF protection, says Green.

For an additional layer of protection, consider wearing UV-protective clothing (called UPF clothing), such as a wide-brimmed hat or wrapping your hair in a scarf. You can also use an umbrella to shield your hair from direct sun exposure and stay out of the sun during the highest UV times of the day (10 a.m. to midafternoon), says DeRosa.

But there are ways to reduce boob sweat and avoid related skin irritation to keep you more comfortable.

What causes boob sweat?

Boob sweat is caused by heat and moisture getting trapped in the skin fold between each breast and the chest, a.k.a. the underboob area. It’s a warm, closed-off  part of the body where heat and moisture can’t evaporate, so sweat easily builds up, says Madeline June, a board-certified nurse practitioner at The Well Westlake. Boob sweat can lead to uncomfortable rashes from chafing (irritation that happens when skin rubs on skin or clothing), or yeast and fungal overgrowth.

Experts told me that several factors exacerbate boob sweat, including high temperatures and humidity levels; hormonal changes, like those that happen during menstruation, pregnancy, perimenopause and menopause; and tight-fitting bras and clothes made from non-breathable fabric.
Can you prevent boob sweat?

No, you can’t completely prevent boob sweat, just like how you can’t completely prevent sweat on any part of your body. “It’s a common issue, not a hygiene failure, and most people experience it at some point,” says Courtney Coons, a board-certified nurse practitioner at PERK Plastic Surgery.
That said, you can use certain products and practice habits that help reduce boob sweat and prevent related skin irritation.

Yes, boob sweat can cause rashes. They’re technically called intertrigo, a type of rash that develops in skin folds, like the ones between the breasts and the chest, says June.
There’s two types of boob sweat rashes to know about:

Heat rashes: When heat stays trapped in the skin fold, it often leads to chafing, which shows up as a raw, irritated rash from the constant friction, says Coons. Moisture rashes: When moisture stays trapped in the skin fold, it can lead to yeast or fungal overgrowth, which shows up as a red, itchy rash, says Coons.

Moisture rashes: When moisture stays trapped in the skin fold, it can lead to yeast or fungal overgrowth, which shows up as a red, itchy rash, says Coons.

To treat rashes from boob sweat, keep the affected area clean, dry and friction-free, says June. Also apply a barrier ointment like petroleum jelly (including Vaseline and Aquaphor) or a zinc oxide cream like Desitin to protect the skin. Topical steroids like hydrocortisone cream can help with itching and inflammation. By following this treatment plan, rashes usually heal within a few days of following this regime, says Coons.

If you don’t treat a rash right away, the irritated, inflamed skin can break down further, leading to open wounds that are more prone to infection, says Coons. Then, when those wounds heal, they can leave behind long-term skin discoloration — hyperpigmentation shows up as dark spots, while hypopigmentation shows us as light spots, says June.

It’s also important to know when to see a doctor about these rashes. Typical irritation presents as mild redness, itching or burning, and the skin is intact without drainage (clear fluid that leaks out of wounds), says June. If your rash isn’t getting better after a week of consistent at-home care, or it’s getting worse and you notice any of the following symptoms, it’s time to see a doctor as you could have an infection, says Coons: persistent redness, spreading redness, warmth, severe itching or burning, open sores with drainage, pain or odor. Your doctor can give you a prescription-strength treatment.

title: Ghost gun recovered in deadly Seattle festival shooting
summary: Seattle officials said that the teen suspect may have been using a ghost gun and that they want to hear from one person who was treated for gunshot wounds.
story: A loaded “ghost gun” was recovered at the scene of a deadly Seattle shooting over the weekend, police said Tuesday as they continue to search for a possible third suspect.

The weapon was found on a 15-year-old who is suspected of being one of the shooters Sunday at the Bite of Seattle food festival, where three people were killed and four were injured. The teen was taken into custody and remains in juvenile detention, according to police.

Ghost guns are firearms that can be assembled at home from parts purchased online. The parts are often obtained without background checks and do not have serial numbers, which would make the guns traceable.

Police found a polymer 89 mm firearm with an extended magazine. It had a 33-round capacity, and 19 rounds remained in the magazine when investigators retrieved it, Police Chief Shon Barnes said at a news conference Tuesday afternoon.
A second gun, which police do not believe was used in the shooting, was found with a full seven rounds in its standard magazine.
Police retrieved a third gun, a Glock Model 45 9 mm pistol with a fully automatic switch. Twenty-one of 40 rounds remained in the magazine, Barnes said.
In total, 14 shell casings from two weapons were found at the scene. The guns had not been reported stolen, police said.
“We have dozens of pieces of digital evidence to review and are continuing to review that information as well as searching the area for more,” Barnes told reporters.
Since Sunday night, the Seattle Police Department has received more than 80 calls to its tip line, Barnes said.

Investigators have said there may have been a third person in the gunbattle, which they say also included the 15-year-old and his 19-year-old “associate,” Junior Cee Niko Semo, who died of multiple gunshot wounds.

The shooting began shortly after 6 p.m. Sunday at the popular food festival, near the famous Space Needle. Two bystanders — Ashley Whitehead, 56, and Carlos Israel Sanchez Villalba, 44 — were killed by gunfire.
Four other people sustained non-life-threatening injuries.

Police said there could be an additional survivor who self-reported to a local hospital with a gunshot wound and then left after having been treated. Because of “legal barriers,” Barnes said, police do not know the person’s identity.

“If you are that person, please reach out to us,” he said. “We would like to make sure, No. 1, that you’re OK, and No. 2, if you would like to speak to an investigator, please reach out to us so we can determine if you may have seen what happened.”

title: Apalachee High School shooter Colt Gray sentenced to life without parole
summary: WINDER, Ga. — The teenager who idolized mass murderers and used the assault-style rifle he got for Christmas to kill two students and two teachers at his Georgia high school will spend the rest of his life in prison.
story: WINDER, Ga. — The teenager who idolized mass murderers and used the assault-style rifle he got for Christmas to kill two students and two teachers at his Georgia high school will spend the rest of his life in prison.

Colt Gray, 16, was sentenced Tuesday to life without parole for the Sept. 4, 2024, shooting at Apalachee High School that also left another teacher and eight more students wounded, seven of them hit by gunfire.
Barrow County Superior Court Judge Nicholas Primm handed down the sentence days after Gray pleaded guilty to all 55 counts against him, including murder.

“You do not seem to be tormented by what you did, you seem to relish following in the footsteps of the murderers you idolize,” Primm told Gray. “You aren’t racked with guilt. You’re proud of yourself.”
Primm added, “There’s no joy here.”
“It’s only a measure of closure,” the judge said. “The slain will not return to life. The injured will not forget their wounds, and a 16-year-old, 16-year-old boy, will live and die in prison.”

Gasps could be heard in the courtroom when the judge handed down the sentence. Before he was led out in handcuffs, Gray glanced quickly up toward the gallery where his grandmother, Debbie Polhamus, had been sitting.
Gray, who was 14 at the time of the shooting, was charged as an adult. His trial had been scheduled to start in mid-October.

But Gray entered the plea without having reached a deal with prosecutors. That left it to the judge to decide whether Gray should be eligible for parole, after hearing victim statements and each side’s summary of a case that has loomed large over the Atlanta suburb of Winder.
Gray declined to address the court at his sentencing hearing Tuesday.

Prosecutors said Gray was obsessed with mass killers and played jailhouse phone conversations with his mother in which he appeared to revel in the attention he received for staging a massacre at the school.

“Four lives were stolen, two of whom were only just beginning,” Primm said. “And it wasn’t done out of fear or anger. You weren’t being bullied at Apalachee. It wasn’t done out of hatred — you didn’t even know anybody at that school. It was done for the infamy of it.”
Teachers Richard “Ricky” Aspinwall, 39, and Cristina Irimie, 53, and students Mason Schermerhorn and Christian Angulo, both 14, died in the shooting.
Their loved ones urged the judge to impose the maximum sentence in victim impact statements delivered in court Friday.

“It is a life sentence of grief and trauma for those left behind,” Aspinwall’s wife, Shayna, told the court. She said their daughters were 2 and 5 when their father was killed and their lives will be “forever marked by his absence.”
Breanna Schermerhorn, whose son Mason was killed, said that while Gray may have been failed by the adults in his life, it was his decision to commit mass murder.
“Those decisions were his and his alone,” she said.

The judge agreed. And he imposed on Gray the same sentence that another judge imposed on another mass murderer the 16-year-old revered — Nikolas Cruz, who was sentenced to life without parole four years ago for the 2018 shooting at a Florida high school that left 14 students and three staff members dead.
“Your plan was not hastily hatched,” Primm said. “It was a slow boil, simmering one in a year’s time. You savored the thought of it. You visualized it, and you fantasized about it.”
“The thought of mimicking these other mass murderers is what brought you joy,” the judge said.
Earlier in the sentencing hearing, a psychologist hired by the defense described the teenager as a “lonely, dysfunctional kid” who had a “chaotic” childhood.
“I thought he was kind of an odd kid,” Kevin Richards said at the sentencing hearing Monday.
His parents abused drugs, had financial problems and fought a lot, Richards said. The family moved frequently and there were long stretches when Gray wasn’t enrolled in school, he said.
So Gray immersed himself online with the “true crime” community and became obsessed with school shootings, Richards said.
Previously, investigators said they found in Colt’s bedroom what they described as a shrine to Cruz.

Gray, investigators said, also became obsessed with the gunmen responsible for the 1999 mass shooting in Colorado at Columbine High School, and the 2012 killings of mostly children at Sandy Hook Elementary School in Connecticut.
Gray was “kind of obsessed” with them, Richards said.

Ashley Gilleland, an investigator with the Barrow County District Attorney’s Office, testified Tuesday that Gray had more than 2,000 photos of Cruz saved on his phone and more photos of Cruz printed and posted on his bedroom wall.
But, Gilleland said, Gray had hoped “to gain some sort of fame or notoriety from” attacking his classmates at school.

To further buttress that argument, the state played recordings of jail calls between Gray and his mother, Marcee Gray, from October and November 2024 during which Gray sounded thrilled to be compared to Cruz and other mass killers.
“I’m in the big leagues, bro,” he said in one call.
Gray’s grandmother testified that her grandson spent long stretches of time with her because his parents were so unstable.
“Well, they always had issues,” Polhamus said. “They were doing a lot of drinking at that time, and then they got way behind on their bills.”

Polhamus said Gray’s dad, Colin Gray, kept dozens of guns in the house and not all of them were locked up. She said he bought Gray the gun he used to attack his classmates in order to bond with his son.
“He really wanted to find something that they could do together,” she said.
Colin Gray was convicted by a jury in March on charges including second-degree murder and involuntary manslaughter for giving his son what turned out to be a multiple murder weapon.

Just before 10 a.m. on the day of the shooting, Gray told his second-period teacher that he needed to see a crisis counselor but instead went to a bathroom to get ready to attack the school, police said.
When he was unable to re-enter his classroom, Gray marched down the hall to another classroom and opened fire and also shot at other people in the hallway, police said.

Gray surrendered to law enforcement officers. In the courtroom, prosecutors played a recording of his interview with investigators during which he sobbed hysterically and repeatedly apologized, calling what he did “horrible” and “the worst nightmare for everyone involved.”
The teenager also described having uncontrollable urges and said he was supposed to see a doctor. “I was so close to getting the help I need and the medication I need,” he told investigators.

But Gray, prosecutors said, had methodically planned the school shooting, and investigators described finding a notebook in which the teen detailed a step-by-step plan on how he would get himself ready in the bathroom.
It also came out in the pretrial investigation that sheriff’s deputies had interviewed Colt and Colin Gray in May 2023 about an online threat linked to the son. Colt Gray denied making the threat.
During Colin Gray’s trial, an investigator testified that he had sought help for his son from a counseling service weeks before the school shooting but failed to follow through.
Marcee Gray, who was separated from Colin Gray, told investigators she had urged her husband weeks before the shooting to secure his guns and restrict their son’s access to them.
Over time, Colin Gray bought the teenager ammunition, a gunsight and other shooting accessories, court records show.
Dan Gallo reported from Winder, Georgia, and Corky Siemaszko reported from New York.

title: Has cyclospora outbreak peaked? There are promising signs in Michigan after lettuce recall.
summary: There are promising signs that illnesses linked to contaminated lettuce may be slowing in Michigan, the hot spot of the multistate outbreak of cyclosporiasis in the U.S.
story: There are promising signs that illnesses linked to contaminated lettuce may be slowing in Michigan, the hot spot of the multistate outbreak of cyclosporiasis in the U.S. That doesn’t mean all the affected produce is gone from stores or restaurants, or that more people aren’t still getting sick, experts say.

On Tuesday, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported more than 18,000 confirmed or suspected nationwide cases of cyclosporiasis, the illness caused by a parasite found in human feces. In nine states, most of the illnesses have been traced to shredded iceberg lettuce sourced from Taylor Farms de Mexico. Other states, such as New York and North Carolina, have also seen higher-than-normal clusters, from unknown sources.
The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services said Tuesday that more than 9,500 people have gotten sick from the parasite in the state, with about 160 hospitalizations, in the last two months.
The Food and Drug Administration didn’t immediately respond to questions about its progress in tracing the source or sources of the illness.
It has been over a week since Taylor Farms voluntarily recalled iceberg lettuce from some Taco Bell restaurants, groceries and food service suppliers.

While the outbreak isn’t over in Michigan, cases may have peaked there. Dr. Natasha Bagdasarian, the state’s chief medical executive, said a significant number of recently reported cases, roughly 475 since Friday, were a result of a reporting delay at one particular healthcare system and don’t necessarily reflect new illnesses.
Bagdasarian said another positive indicator they are seeing is that the percentage of visits to emergency departments with diarrhea as a main complaint is slowing.
However, people with milder symptoms may not be getting tested.

“I do have a big caveat,” said Bagdasarian. “We have heard recently from some of our health systems that because of backlogs in their labs, and because of limitations with testing supplies, they have been limiting tests to those who are severely ill, or those who are immunocompromised.”
Because of this limitation, investigators in Michigan are unsure about the projected spread of cyclospora, especially if other, unidentified culprits are still in the food supply.
“I don’t know if a single product recall is related to the slowdown that we’ve seen,” said Bagdasarian.

While the purportedly contaminated lettuce has been recalled, Bagdasarian also credited public health interventions, such as guidance to peel, cook and remove the outer layers of produce, for the slowdown.
Bagdasarian said it’s up to the federal health agencies to trace, test and find the contaminated produce, based on interviews with patients and other data gathering.

“There are a fair number of folks out there who have not reported eating lettuce or who have not reported eating at any particular fast-food restaurant,” she said. “So I don’t know, based on my data, that I can think this is exclusively lettuce or whether there are other things going on, especially knowing that there are multiple other outbreaks happening across the United States.”
Health officials don’t have access to real-time genetic sequencing, which makes it harder to match a contaminated product to a specific case.

Jennifer McEntire, the founder of Food Safety Strategy, a consulting firm, said it’s also difficult to pinpoint a specific source because many products “move or change hands many times, go through numerous distribution centers [and] sometimes brokers.”

Health officials have suspected other food sources in this season’s outbreaks, namely cilantro and parsley, but have not confirmed either one. In New York, state officials investigated an earlier, smaller cluster of cyclosporiasis cases in April and traced the outbreak to cilantro served at a Brooklyn restaurant, though they never definitively confirmed it was the source.

Last week, officials in North Carolina — which has reported 561 cyclospora cases — said their preliminary investigation suggests cilantro and parsley could be behind those cases. Neither state’s outbreaks have been linked to Taylor Farms lettuce.

Dr. Stephen Ostroff, a former acting FDA commissioner, said it’s possible other illnesses could stem from contaminated lettuce that was grown in the same region as Taylor Farms de Mexico and was also served in the U.S.
Frank Yiannas, former deputy commissioner for food policy and response at the FDA, said it’s clear there is more than one product causing illnesses.

“If, in fact, all the lettuce is pulled from the market, consumers should not be surprised that they continue to see states report illnesses, and they identify food vehicles other than lettuce,” he said.

In Michigan, there have been two distinct waves of cyclospora, which tends to be a summer problem in the U.S. This year, the first wave peaked June 21 through June 28, and again July 5 through July 12, Bagdasarian said.

Barbara Kowalcyk, director of the Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security at George Washington University, believes that’s because the contaminated product was supplied in two separate batches.
“If you have ongoing contamination of irrigation water or processing water, then you will see the outbreak going on,” she said.
“So the question that raises in my mind is: Is there a larger contamination event in that part of the country?” Kowalcyk said, referring to the Taylor Farms site in central Mexico.
Contaminated water has the potential to spread to different crops and multiple batches of products.
“There’s still a lot that we don’t know,” said Kowalcyk. “This goes back to the need for better laboratory methods in terms of detecting cyclospora in the environment.”
Kowalcyk said that the continued search for the source of the cyclospora outbreak highlights vulnerabilities in the U.S.’ public health system, a result of a lack of funding.
“We still need increased capacity. We aren’t investing enough in science. We’re not investing enough in research,” Kowalcyk said.

title: Search for North Carolina woman Liz Waddell is still a missing person case, Grenada police say
summary: Grenadian police said their nearly week-old search for a missing North Carolina woman is still active, with hopes of finding the swimmer alive.
story: Grenadian police said Tuesday that their nearly week-old search for a missing North Carolina woman is still active, with hopes of finding the swimmer alive.
Elizabeth “Liz” Waddell, a 44-year-old Cary resident, was last seen going out for a swim at Grand Anse Beach on Wednesday, the Royal Grenada Police Force said.

“At this time, the matter continues, continues to be treated as a missing person investigation,” acting Commissioner of Police Randy Connaught told reporters Tuesday. “I repeat, at this time, the matter continues to be treated as a missing person.”
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
Surveillance cameras captured Waddell walking on a jetty near the water at 11:36 a.m. the morning she went missing, Connaught said.
She went into the water at 11:51 a.m. and more footage captured her swimming under the jetty at 12:04 p.m., the police official said.
Witnesses have told investigators they later saw Waddell in the open water, police said.
Waddell’s traveling partner was captured on surveillance cameras on the beach at 12:46 p.m. and she reported the swimmer missing to police at 5:50 p.m., Connaught added.
“There is nothing questionable about her account of the investigations and we continue to receive cooperation from her,”  Connaught said of the traveling companion.
Even though Waddell hasn’t been seen in nearly six days, police said they still seek to rescue her.
“It is our hope that Elizabeth will be found and found alive and well,” Connaught said. “The Royal Grenada Police Force remains equally hopeful that she will be safe and that she is safe.”
Local police had been appealing to fishermen, boat operators and residents along the southern coastline to keep their eyes peeled for medium-build woman with short blond hair.
Waddell and her friend first arrived in Grenada, the island nation in the eastern Caribbean Sea that’s about 100 miles north of Venezuela, on July 11.
The missing woman’s husband has since come to the island to help in the search effort, officials said.

“Any bit of information will do at this time, and we do hope that we can locate Elizabeth very soon,” Connaught said. “Again, we empathize with the family, relatives and friends, and we are hopeful that Elizabeth will be found alive. Thank you.”

title: Trump asks Supreme Court to overturn $83.3 million award in E. Jean Carroll defamation case
summary: Lawyers for President Donald Trump argued that he had immunity for statements made while president.
story: President Donald Trump is again asking the Supreme Court to intervene in his yearslong legal battle with writer E. Jean Carroll, this time arguing that he should not have to pay an $83.3 million jury award on the grounds of presidential immunity.

Lawyers for Trump urged the high court to review the case and consider overturning the jury’s ruling in 2024 that found he defamed Carroll after he repeatedly denied that he sexually abused her in a dressing room in 1996.

“This is the first case in our Nation’s history in which a court has imposed damages liability on a President for his conduct in office,” Trump’s lawyers wrote in the filing, calling the $83.3 million award “exorbitant.”
“If left standing, the decision below will cause significant damage, not only to this President and future Presidents, but also to ‘the Nation that the Presidency was designed to serve,’” they wrote.

Carroll sued Trump in 2019 over allegations that he defamed her during his first term in office, including when he said she made up the allegations of sexual abuse to sell more copies of her upcoming book.

Trump’s lawyers argued Tuesday that under the Westfall Act, a federal statute that protects government employees from certain lawsuits while they are engaged in their official duties, Trump should be able to swap out his name as the defendant in the case and replace it with the U.S. government.
If it is applied, the act would essentially nullify Carroll’s case, since the U.S. government cannot be sued for defamation.

“Here, the president of the United States has been ordered to pay nearly $100 million in damages ... for issuing a press release and answering reporters’ questions, from the White House, defending against attacks on his fitness for office,” the filing said.

Trump’s lawyers argued that the “threat of even a single damages judgment based on official acts will render all Presidents ‘unable to boldly and fearlessly carry out [their] duties for fear that [they] may be next.’”
Trump asked a federal appeals court to consider his argument for presidential immunity in the case in April when his lawyers requested a rehearing before a full bench of judges.
The appeals court denied the request, as did a three-judge panel that rejected an appeal from Trump in September that was based on presidential immunity.
Trump’s lawyers pushed back against the appeals court’s ruling in the filing Tuesday, citing the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision on presidential immunity.

The filing said the appeals court “refused to apply Presidential immunity even after this Court recognized that ‘most of a President’s public communications are likely to fall comfortably within’ that protection.”
Carroll’s legal team declined to comment on the petition Tuesday evening.
The Supreme Court denied Trump’s request last month to review a separate successful defamation lawsuit filed by Carroll.

That case, which was filed in 2022 after her initial lawsuit was delayed by legal questions, focused on the sexual abuse itself and on claims that Trump defamed her after he left office. A jury awarded Carroll $5 million in the second case in 2023.
Carroll collected the award from that judgment this month after Trump tried repeatedly to block the payment in court. Trump has denied all wrongdoing in both cases.

title: Karlie Kloss Calls Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce an ‘Amazing Couple’ After Going to Their Wedding: EXCLUSIVE
summary: Karlie Kloss opened up to TODAY about her new book and said that Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce are an “amazing couple.’
story: Weeks after being photographed heading to Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s wedding in New York, Karlie Kloss opened up about the nuptials.

“Listen, I try to protect the privacy of my friends’ personal lives,” Kloss said during an appearance on TODAY on July 28. “But what I will say is that they’re an amazing couple and I’m so happy for them.”

Swift and Kelce’s wedding unfolded on July 3 in New York, drawing a star-studded crowd to Madison Square Garden. While most of the wedding has been kept secret, guests have shared a few details, like handkerchiefs embroidered with a T&T logo and who, exactly, caught the bouquet.

Kloss and Swift met at a fashion show in 2013, Swift confirmed to Vogue in 2015, and became fast friends. The two shared bits of their friendship with the world and the press. Kloss even appeared in Swift’s “Bad Blood” music video in 2015.

However, the two have not been photographed or seen together publicly since 2016. Swift did not attend either of Kloss’ wedding ceremonies to Joshua Kushner in 2018 and 2019. Of their friendship, a 2018 New York Times profile of Kloss said, “Despite internet gossip suggesting otherwise, the pair continues to be good friends and they talk frequently.”

Kloss, meanwhile, is interested in untangling a different type of problem. Over a decade ago, the former supermodel started a non-profit technology education program, Kode With Klossy, a camp that connects young girls with opportunities and support in the technology and computer science space.
Her first children’s book, “Spaghetti Code: A Story About Problem-Solving, Pasta, and the Power of Big Ideas,” out July 28, introduces coding concepts to 4 to 8-year-olds.

“‘Spaghetti code’ is a term that means when your code is a hot mess. There’s a bug in there somewhere and you’ve got to fix it,” Kloss said on TODAY. “The idea is to not get frustrated or overwhelmed when you hit a mistake, but to work through it and keep going.”
The mom of three called her leap into writing a children’s picture book about coding principles a “tall order,” but wanted it to be “really fun and visual.”
“‘Spaghetti Code’ is really inspired by our scholars, who are these incredible, passionate young women from around the world,” Kloss said.
“Spaghetti Code” is the first in a five-book series, per Publisher’s Weekly.

title: John Mulaney Announces 9 New York City Shows: EXCLUSIVE
summary: John Mulaney has revealed he will perform at nine New York City venues over nine straight days, ending with a performance at Madison Square Garden.
story: He’s already conquered the Windy City — now John Mulaney has his eyes set on the Big Apple.

Mulaney, who became the first comedian to headline Chicago’s Wrigley Field during a July 11 show, has announced “Mulaney Takes Manhattan,” a series of nine shows over nine days in New York City, culminating with a performance at Madison Square Garden, he revealed exclusively on TODAY on July 28.

“Instead of doing one show in New York City, or even three shows in New York City, for my tour, I’m going to do a very special run. Nine different iconic New York City venues in nine nights,” he said.

“This is very, very cool, I must say. I’m doing something very cool, and I’m a very cool person,” he joked. “This is really a great way to do the intimate small places. I love playing here, building up to Madison Square Garden, doing Radio City (Music Hall). I filmed a special at Radio City, to go back there. It’s going to be really cool.”
The shows, which will begin Jan. 7, 2027 and end Jan. 15, 2027, will feature special guests and a new experience each performance.
You can sign up for a chance to get tickets at johnmulaney.com.
Here’s a look at all of the shows.
